anchors.quote: on the first pass probably about 30 seconds

claim_en: On the first pass the recruiter spends about 30 seconds on a CV.

anchors.quote: the recruiter isn't really trying to understand the entire career at that point they're trying to really establish whether that's enough relevant experience to justify carrying on reading

claim_en: The first pass is not an attempt to understand the whole career; it only establishes whether there is enough relevant experience to justify reading on.

anchors.quote: I'd look at the most recent experience first if it's in date order um you know what you've been doing what technologies you've been using how closely does that match with the problem that the company is trying to solve
I'd scan for recent and relevant experience rather than expecting a system to decide whether someone was good or not

claim_en: The recruiter reads the most recent experience first and checks how closely its technologies match the problem the company is trying to solve; with many applications, the recruiter scans for recent and relevant experience.

anchors.quote: if I can't see a technical fit on page one it's you know it's difficult to keep going when you'got a sea of applications to get through

claim_en: If the recruiter cannot see a technical fit on page one, it is hard to keep reading with a sea of applications to get through.

anchors.quote: the recruiter would review inbound applications or then actively search for somebody through like LinkedIn or a job board or their network if the profile looks relevant the next step would usually be a phone screening

claim_en: Recruiters review inbound applications or search LinkedIn, job boards and their network; a relevant profile usually leads to a phone screening.

anchors.quote: I wasn't really looking for somebody to repeat their CV on that phone screening i wanted to know whether they could back up whatever was written in their CV you know what was the problem what did you personally do what changed because of your work
on that first phone screening that's why it's important to understand not just the tech you've worked on but what problems you solved

claim_en: In the phone screening the recruiter does not want the CV repeated but checks whether the candidate can back up what it says: the problem, their personal part and what changed; that is why the screen asks about the problems solved, not just the technologies.

anchors.quote: the recruiter must be able to explain internally why you're worth meeting so we you know we have people to report to we have to justify why a person is right

claim_en: The recruiter has to justify internally why each candidate introduced to the hiring manager is worth meeting.

anchors.quote: i never relied heavily on an ATS to make any kind of hiring decisions

claim_en: In the recruiter's own practice the ATS was never relied on heavily for hiring decisions.
notes: The recruiter stresses this is personal experience and that it varies between organizations.

anchors.quote: the main exception was any kind of hard requirement so like security clearance would often be needed you know you'd need the ATS to filter anybody that wasn't SC eligible

claim_en: In the recruiter's own experience, the one exception to not relying on the ATS was using it to screen out applicants who failed a hard requirement, such as security clearance eligibility.

anchors.quote: candidates definitely shouldn't ignore key words because you know recruiters still need to find them
you should definitely optimize your CV to be found

claim_en: Do not ignore keywords: recruiters still need to find the CV, so optimize it to be found.

anchors.quote: they also shouldn't write a CV for a robot and then it makes it unreadable for a human
rather than just DevOps Kubernetes Python do you know what I mean rather than just buzzword buzzwords everywhere
but write it to be understood

claim_en: Do not write the CV for a robot: buzzword lists make it unreadable for the human who needs to understand the job and the problems solved.

anchors.quote: technical fit is is immediately obvious on page one if I'm recruiting for like a React engineer I shouldn't have to search through pages to find the React experience
make the match easy to see and never expect a recruiter to to work it out for you
look at the first page of your CV does it clearly show the skills that are required by those roles
make your technical fit obvious on page one

claim_en: Make the technical fit obvious on page one: a recruiter hiring for a React engineer should not have to search through pages for the React experience, or work out the match.

anchors.quote: don't simply give me a list of technologies tell me what you're building what problem you're solving your personal contribution and the result

under each project and each career uh entry you should put you know the topic so fintech or financial services or healthcare this was the problem this is what we were solving these were our end customers
are you showing achievements and problem solved or like just merely listing responsibilities
show the projects that you'delivered don't just show that you know a technology um show the problems you've solved

claim_en: Instead of a list of technologies, say what you were building, the problem it solved, your personal contribution and the result; under each role give the domain, the problem and the end customers.

anchors.quote: candidate had strong full stack foundations but the client needed uh react and the profile showed view much more clearly um so the person is probably great probably very capable but the evidence that the hiring manager needed wasn't visible enough

claim_en: In a recent case on the employer side, a capable full stack candidate lost out because the CV showed Vue more clearly than the React the client needed: the evidence was not visible enough.
notes: "view" in the quote is Vue, mis-transcribed. A separate assertion from the page-one reading habit (a case, not a practice), so not folded into it.

anchors.quote: the first one I would definitely say is length most CVs don't need to document every task from every do job someone has ever had

claim_en: The first of the three biggest CV mistakes the recruiter sees is length: most CVs do not need to document every task from every job.

anchors.quote: the second is poor presentation i think a recruiter or anybody looking at your CV you know the recipient on the other end needs to be able to navigate the document quickly so like fancy graphics they're not really necessary at that point it's more about clarity

claim_en: The second biggest mistake the recruiter sees is poor presentation: the reader must navigate the CV quickly, so fancy graphics are unnecessary and clarity is what counts.

anchors.quote: the third I would probably say is is listing technologies without explaining the project or or your contribution so um Java AWS Kubernetes tells me very little you know what did you build what was difficult what did you own what improved

claim_en: The third biggest mistake the recruiter sees is listing technologies without explaining the project or the candidate's contribution: what was built, what was difficult, what was owned, what improved.

anchors.quote: a genuine concern that I would have would be somebody who had been out of work for a long period but couldn't show any learning or projects or effort to remain current
the gap itself isn't really the problem to be honest with you because everybody has gaps in their employment but it's what the person did

claim_en: A gap itself is not the problem, since everybody has gaps; the recruiter's concern is a long time out of work with no learning, projects or effort to stay current.

anchors.quote: I don't think there's a a right number but I would say maximum absolute maximum five pages
if you're somebody with 10 to 15 years experience you can definitely have five pages to capture your your experience
if your CV is two or three pages great
I guess between between like two and five would be a good number

claim_en: There is no right page count, but two to five pages is a good range and five pages is the absolute maximum; with 10 to 15 years of experience five pages is fine, and two or three pages is fine early in a career.

anchors.quote: i think a one pager probably wouldn't capture enough and also I think when you receive a onepage CV I'm not sure the kind of message that that sends to the recruiter
you want to be able to capture enough information that's going to make them want to scroll down to page two and three

claim_en: A one-page CV probably does not capture enough, and it may send the recruiter the wrong message; the CV should make the reader want to scroll to pages two and three.

anchors.quote: page one you know You can have a section where you list your technologies because you know you want to be able to show whoever's reading your CV that you'got the required skill set

claim_en: Page one can have a section listing technologies, to show the reader the required skill set.

anchors.quote: you don't just want a bunch of technologies listed there if they're already on page one great let the recruiter assume that you've used those technologies across different projects
you can like sprinkle in the kind of tech you use
don't then list every technology on every project
you don't need to list every single technology that you worked on in every single project

claim_en: Do not repeat the technology list under each role: if the stack is on page one, let the recruiter assume it was used across projects and mention tech only within the description of the work.

anchors.quote: first check whether you're genuinely applying for roles that fit your experience
more applications probably aren't the solution
don't make the mistake of thinking that applying for more jobs automatically improves your chances it's not necessarily a volume game

claim_en: When applications bring no interviews, first check that the roles really fit your experience; applying for everything does no good and more applications are not the solution.

anchors.quote: is your location and right to work position obvious
my advice on this topic would be to remove uncertainty wherever you can so be clear about your right to work your location your availability
be transparent about your location and visa situation

claim_en: Check that the CV makes the candidate's location and right-to-work position obvious.

anchors.quote: LinkedIn and networking and referrals they can actually be a bit more important than the CV because they help you escape the application queue

claim_en: LinkedIn, networking and referrals can matter more than the CV, because they let the candidate escape the application queue.

anchors.quote: if somebody went out of their way to send me a thoughtful and relevant message I would notice it
a short message explaining why their background matched my role or my company um that's powerful

claim_en: The recruiter noticed a short, thoughtful message explaining why the sender's background matched the role or company, as opposed to a request to find them a job.

anchors.quote: a referral transfers some of the trust as well um it doesn't guarantee an interview or a job obviously but a hiring manager or somebody can look at your profile a bit more carefully

claim_en: A referral transfers some trust: it guarantees nothing, but a hiring manager can look at the profile a bit more carefully.

anchors.quote: a lot of the placements that that I would make in my early career all came from referrals i would say probably as much as like 70%

claim_en: In the recruiter's early career, up to about 70% of placements came from referrals.

anchors.quote: I personally wouldn't bother with a traditional cover letter unless obviously like you just said they were specifically asking for one

claim_en: Do not bother with a traditional cover letter unless the employer specifically asks for one.

anchors.quote: i would rather see three or four strong sentences at the top of a CV explaining who you are what you specialize in and why you're a fit for that type of opportunity
you're going to have to tailor that to 50 applications but it's much better to do across three or four sentences than an entire cover letter

claim_en: Rather than a cover letter, put three or four strong sentences at the top of the CV, tailored per application: who you are, what you specialize in and why you fit the opportunity.

anchors.quote: if you're changing careers if you're relocating or you need to explain something unusual a short tailored note can really help you don't need a whole page cover letter

claim_en: When changing careers, relocating or explaining something unusual, a short tailored note can really help, though not a whole-page cover letter.

anchors.quote: a generic page describing how passionate and hardworking you are it adds very little
I want to see something that's like personal like you've done your research you've looked at the job you've looked at the company
I'd rather see that than a cover letter that probably wouldn't get read

claim_en: A generic page about being passionate and hardworking adds very little; the recruiter would rather see research into the job, the company and its values than a cover letter that probably would not get read.

anchors.quote: it could be right to work could be sponsorship could be salary requirements could be relocation time scale could be family circumstances could be language time zone payroll background checks
it's important early that a recruiter understands not only whether the candidate can do the job but whether the practical route to employing them is actually possible

claim_en: For overseas candidates the recruiter used the screening call to settle early whether employing them is practically possible: right to work, sponsorship, salary, relocation timing, family, language, time zone, payroll and background checks.

anchors.quote: sponsorship is probably the hardest practical barrier to overcome

if somebody already has the right to work for an existing visa uh the conversation is is way way easier if they depend entirely on the employer sponsoring them number of available organizations shrinks massively

claim_en: Sponsorship is the hardest practical barrier: with an existing right to work the conversation is far easier, while depending entirely on sponsorship shrinks the number of possible employers massively.

anchors.quote: probably not on the CV um because then that introduces bias in the whole selection process

claim_en: Probably do not mention needing sponsorship on the CV, because it introduces bias into the selection process.

anchors.quote: it should be clear on the application or during the first recruiter conversation
hiding it until the final interview just wastes everybody's time

claim_en: Raise the sponsorship need early, on the application or in the first recruiter conversation; hiding it until the final interview wastes everybody's time and undermines trust.

anchors.quote: explain your position accurately but confidently as well what permissions you currently have when it expires is a big one that you need to remember and then exactly what support you would need

claim_en: Explain the visa position accurately and confidently: the permissions held, when they expire and exactly what support is needed.

anchors.quote: things come out in conversation where you know both parties can make it work whereas if you put it on your CV um it gives people a reason to to click past

claim_en: Stating a sponsorship need on the CV gives screeners a reason to click past it, while in conversation both sides can often make it work.

anchors.quote: nationality should never be a judgment about somebody's ability character suitability

the reality unfortunately is that candidates are probably going to encounter practical obstacles so sponsorship relocation financial or security processes employers that are just cautious about that particular region

claim_en: Candidates from some regions are likely to meet practical obstacles (sponsorship, relocation, financial or security processes, cautious employers), even though nationality should never be a judgment of ability.
notes: The recruiter notes limited experience with Iranian candidates specifically.

anchors.quote: focus on internationally minded employers
target companies that can realistically hire you

claim_en: Target employers that can realistically hire you, such as internationally minded ones.

anchors.quote: build relationships with people that can actually see your ability before they see any kind of administration complication
build relationships rather than relying exclusively on applications

claim_en: Build relationships with people who can see your ability before they see any administrative complication, rather than relying only on applications.
notes: Advice for international candidates; distinct from the c001 claim that networking can matter more than the CV.

anchors.quote: i think sometimes but uh usually because of the employer's operating constraints rather than the engineers talent

claim_en: Location sometimes matters, usually because of the employer's operating constraints (regulated data, time zone overlap, legal entities, payroll, security) rather than the engineer's talent.

anchors.quote: I think it's a good question for candidates to ask and show that they're bought into the process like is my location a hard restriction or is there a practical concern that I can help you address

claim_en: Candidates can ask whether their location is a hard restriction or a practical concern they can help address; it shows they are bought into the process.

anchors.quote: improve your LinkedIn profile show that you're active rather than invisible
there's nothing worse than coming across a LinkedIn profile and there's no picture there's like one job history mentioned on there but there's no bio

claim_en: Improve the LinkedIn profile and show activity: nothing is worse than a profile with no picture, one job, no bio, no comments and no posts.

anchors.quote: that's not me telling you to go post AI slop on LinkedIn please don't do that

claim_en: Being active on LinkedIn does not mean posting AI-generated content the candidate did not write.
